messages.text: My wife and I are retired. We get about $2,600 a month from Social Security together. Any food help for us?

I can already say some things. I need two more answers before I can tell you more.

**What I found so far**
- The new federal food assistance (SNAP) numbers started October 1, 2026. For a 2-person household, the **monthly income limit after deductions is about $1,804**. The most food help a 2-person household can get is about **$562 a month**. The standard deduction is $217. The lowest monthly benefit is $25. I got these figures from [Propel's summary of the 2026-27 USDA update](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/). I couldn't open USDA's own page, so please treat them as approximate. USDA's [official notice](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf) should have the exact numbers.
- Your $2,600 is over the usual "income before taxes" limit for 2 people (about $2,345). **But Tennessee's rules say that if someone in the home is 60 or older, or disabled, only the "after deductions" test applies.** Tennessee Human Services policy says this, as shown in my search results. I couldn't open the page itself ([TDHS policy 24.14](https://TN.gov/content/dam/tn/human-services/documents/24.14%20SNAP%20Income.pdf)).
- Tennessee's income limit is also unclear right now. The official rule says 130% of poverty, but some reports say 200%. If it's 200%, your income would likely fit.

**So food help is possible for you.** It mostly depends on your bills. Deductions can bring your counted income down.

**Two questions:**
1. Are you both 60 or older? Does either of you have a disability?
2. How much do you pay each month for rent or mortgage? Do you pay for heating or cooling separately? Do you also pay for medical bills (like premiums, prescriptions, or doctor visits)?

With those answers I can give you a better idea and a rough monthly amount. Only the Tennessee Department of Human Services can decide. You can apply either way.

Yeah, we're both over 60. Neither of us has a disability.

Rent is $900. We pay heating and cooling on our own, usually around $150 a month depending on the season. Our medical out-of-pocket is about $30 a month total.

**It looks unlikely for food assistance (SNAP), but possibly. You can still apply.**

**How I worked it out (estimate only)**
- Your income before taxes is $2,600. Taking off the $217 standard deduction leaves about $2,383.
- Your $30 in medical costs is under the $35 a month that is ignored, so it doesn't lower your income.
- Your housing and utility costs are about $1,050 a month ($900 rent plus $150 for heating and cooling). That is less than half of your $2,383, so it adds no extra deduction. Tennessee may use a set utility amount instead of your real bills. I couldn't find that number. Even a fairly large one wouldn't change the result.
- Your counted income would be about $2,300 to $2,400. The limit for 2 people is about $1,804, so you'd be over it. Your housing costs would have to be around $1,770 a month to get under it. (Source: [Propel's summary of the 2026-27 USDA figures](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/). I couldn't open USDA's own page.)

**Why I'm not saying "no"**
- Tennessee's income limit is unsettled. The official rule is 130% of poverty, but some reports say 200%. At 200%, your income might fit.
- Even then, the benefit would be small. The most a 2-person household can get is about $562. Your income would cut that to about the lowest benefit, **around $25 a month**. This is a rough estimate, and the state decides the real amount.

**Things that could change this**
- If your medical costs go above $35 a month, the part over $35 can be deducted. That includes premiums, prescriptions, and doctor visits. Keep your receipts.
- The state counts your real income, so report it accurately on the application. Overpayments have to be paid back.
- There is a savings limit. I haven't confirmed what it is for households with someone 60 or older.

**Next steps**
- **Apply online or ask questions:** [Tennessee Department of Human Services](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices.html). I couldn't open their SNAP page, so please check it for the current phone number and application link.
- **Free local help:** call **211**. They can help you apply and tell you about other help for seniors, like food pantries and home-delivered meals.

Only the Tennessee Department of Human Services can decide if you get food assistance and how much. Applying is free, and it's the only way to know for sure.

Sources:
- [Propel: SNAP 2026-27 cost-of-living increase](https://www.propel.app/snap/snap-2026-2027-cola-increase/)
- [TDHS Policy 24.14, SNAP Income](https://TN.gov/content/dam/tn/human-services/documents/24.14%20SNAP%20Income.pdf). This came up in my search, but I couldn't open it.
- [USDA 2027 cost-of-living memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf). This also came up in my search, but I couldn't open it.

The USDA's official FY2027 memo, dated August 21, 2026, sets the new SNAP figures, effective October 1, 2026.

- **Maximum allotments:** For a family of four in the 48 contiguous states and D.C., the maximum is $1,023, up from $994 in FY2026 (The maximum allotment for a family of four in the 48 States and D.C., will be $1,023. ). A one-person household moves from $298 to $306 (A single-person household moves from $298 to $306, and the minimum monthly benefit climbs from $24 to $25.). Alaska's four-person range is $1,306 to $2,027. Hawaii's four-person maximum falls, from $1,689 to $1,655 (Hawaii's maximum allotment for a family of four is actually falling, from $1,689 to $1,655), according to a third-party site.
- **Income limits:** The USDA memo includes gross monthly tables at 130% and 165% of poverty for elderly/disabled separate households, and its figures appear in the memo's tables. For the 165% table in the 48 states, D.C., Guam, and the Virgin Islands, one person is $2,195 and four people is $4,538 (Gross Monthly Income Eligibility Standards for Households Where Elderly Disabled Are a Separate Household (165 Percent of Poverty Level)). The 130% gross limits for other households are shown in a third-party summary as $1,729 for one person and $2,345 for two (1 person: $1,729 (up from $1,696) 2 people: $2,345 (up from $2,292)). I could not confirm the four-person 130% figure from the official memo in these results.
- **Deductions:** The standard deduction for households of one to three rises from $209 to $217 in the 48 states and D.C., and the maximum excess shelter deduction rises from $744 to $789 (The standard deduction for a household of one to three people increases from $209 to $217 in the 48 states and D.C. • Higher shelter deduction: The maximum excess shelter deduction increases from $744 to $789 in the 48 states and D.C.). These come from a secondary news source; I did not see the memo's deduction table in the results.

Caveats: Most of the detail comes from secondary sites, and the USDA memo excerpt I saw was partial. Some sites also mention state-level rules, such as broad-based categorical eligibility, that can raise gross income limits above the federal standards. For exact figures, use the USDA memo at the government source.

The official Tennessee sources agree on the core rule: elderly and disabled households face only the net income test, while the dollar figures I found vary across sites.

- **Official policy:** TDHS Policy 24.14 says an elderly or disabled household must meet only the net income eligibility standards, and the gross standard does not apply to households that contain elderly or disabled household members.
- **Tennessee rule:** Rule 1240-01-14-.09 applies the 130% gross limit only to households without an elderly or disabled member, and it says all households including households containing an elderly or disabled member are subject to the net monthly income standards.
- **Dollar amounts conflict:** A legal-information site lists 2026 limits (October 2025 to September 2026) of 1 person: $1,696 gross / $1,305 net and 4 people: $3,483 gross / $2,680 net. Another site gives a 4-person gross limit of $3,575/mo, and its 4-person net limit of $2,750/mo. I could not confirm which figures match the current federal table, so check the TDHS or USDA FNS tables before relying on any number.
- **Asset test:** One site says households with a member aged 60 or older, or a disabled member have a higher resource limit, but another puts the figure at 3,500 if a household member is age 60 or older, or is disabled. These figures conflict, so verify them too.

I didn't find Tennessee's specific heating/cooling standard utility allowance dollar amount for October 2026, so I can't confirm that figure from these results.

What the results do cover:

- **Tennessee uses a fixed allowance.** One source says the state applies a set allowance for households with heating or cooling costs, instead of tallying actual bills (Tennessee also uses a standard utility allowance in place of requiring you to document every individual utility bill. If you pay heating or cooling costs, the state applies a set allowance to your shelter calculation rather than adding up your actual bills.).
- **Federal rules changed.** A December 2024 USDA memo says the final rule set requirements for how states build their allowances, and that State agencies have until October 1, 2025, to ensure SUA values comply with the new methodology requirements. The rule also sets the largest standard at the 80th percentile of low-income households' utility costs in the state (per the 2019 proposed rule summary, the heating and cooling standard utility allowance (HCSUA) at the 80th percentile of low-income households' utility costs in the state). Because values are meant to be updated, the current Tennessee figure should be checked against the state's own SNAP policy or the USDA FNS SUA tables.
- **Pending legislation.** H.R. 7069 (Affordable Food and Energy Act of 2026) would widen SUA eligibility to households receiving energy assistance. As of the source's listing, it was Active· Referred to the Subcommittee on Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture.
- **Federal FY2026 figures.** The FY2026 maximum allotments run from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026, so they will roll over to new FY2027 figures on October 1, 2026. The Tennessee maximum for a household of four was listed at $975 (one third-party site), and the excess shelter deduction is capped at $744 for most households.

Recommended next step: check the Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP policy manual or the USDA FNS state SUA table for the exact October 2026 heating/cooling amount.
